title: Kinetic modelling of growth and storage molecule production in microalgae under mixotrophic and autotrophic conditions.

Kinetic modelling of growth and storage molecule production in
microalgae under mixotrophic and autotrophic conditions
Victoria O. Adesanya a,⇑, Matthew P. Davey b, Stuart A. Scott a, Alison G. Smith b
a Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge, Trumpington Street, Cambridge CB2 1PZ, United Kingdom

h i g h l i g h t s
 Algal cultures were modelled under mixotrophic and autotrophic growth conditions.
 The kinetic model was developed as a function of nitrogen, carbon and light supply.
 The model is based on the Droop model and carbon balance within an algal cell.
 Starch and TAG are the main storage components produced under nitrogen limitation.
 Biomass concentration and storage content were highest under mixotrophic condition.

In order to improve algal biofuel production on a commercial-scale, an understanding of algal growth and
fuel molecule accumulation is essential. A mathematical model is presented that describes biomass
growth and storage molecule (TAG lipid and starch) accumulation in the freshwater microalga Chlorella
vulgaris, under mixotrophic and autotrophic conditions. Biomass growth was formulated based on the
Droop model, while the storage molecule production was calculated based on the carbon balance within
the algal cells incorporating carbon ﬁxation via photosynthesis, organic carbon uptake and functional
biomass growth. The model was validated with experimental growth data of C. vulgaris and was found
to ﬁt the data well. Sensitivity analysis showed that the model performance was highly sensitive to vari-
ations in parameters associated with nutrient factors, photosynthesis and light intensity. The maximum
productivity and biomass concentration were achieved under mixotrophic nitrogen sufﬁcient conditions,
while the maximum storage content was obtained under mixotrophic nitrogen deﬁcient conditions.

1. Introduction
Microalgae have diverse industrial applications either as total
biomass or after extraction of speciﬁc chemicals ranging from food,
pharmaceuticals, cosmetics and high value products (astaxanthin
and b-carotene) to wastewater treatment in bioremediation, and
carbon capture and sequestration (Mata et al., 2010). Increased
knowledge that total reliance on fossil fuel is unsustainable due
to the fast depletion of oil reserves, ﬂuctuations in oil prices and
environmental deterioration from the emission of green house
gases has led to active research on alternative renewable and
sustainable energy sources (Adesanya et al., 2012). In particular,
microalgal-based biofuels have received signiﬁcant interest due
to possible beneﬁts over ﬁrst and second generation biomass
feedstocks. Some of the merits of algal feedstock for bioenergy
production include: high growth rate and short generation time,
no competition with food crops for arable land, use of wastewater
as a source of nutrients, and high storage molecule (in the form of
TAG lipid and starch) accumulation under certain growth condi-
tions (Chisti 2007; Schenk et al., 2008; Scott et al., 2010). Algal bio-
fuel production could also be integrated with coal ﬁred plants or
other ﬂue gas sources to capture emitted carbon dioxide. Algal bio-
mass can be converted through different metabolic pathways to
generate biofuels such as biodiesel, bioethanol, biohydrogen, bio-
gas, biogasoline and bio-oil (Singh and Gu, 2010). Although the al-
gae-to-fuel technology has a potential to compete with fossil fuels,
commercial scale production is yet to be realized since the produc-
tion cost is not low enough to be competitive in the market (Siaut
et al., 2011). This study focuses on the two main storage molecules
used in algal biofuel; TAG for biodiesel production via transesteri-
ﬁcation and starch for bioethanol production via fermentation.
Microalgal genera exhibit considerable versatile and ﬂexible
metabolic activities, which make many of them adaptable to

the biotechnological industry, providing a platform to modify, con-
trol and maximise the formation of a targeted compound within
the algal cell. The various types of algal metabolism that have been
reported include autotrophic, heterotrophic, mixotrophic and pho-
toheterotrophic (Mata et al., 2010). Photoautotrophic cultivation
for algal biofuel production is technically feasible with the added
incentive of CO2 capture, thus potentially contributing to global
CO2 reduction. However, this culture mode is generally character-
ised by low biomass concentrations due to light attenuation and
mutual shading of cells in dense cultures (Abreu et al., 2012).
Heterotrophic cultivation eliminates the requirement for light
and has the potential to signiﬁcantly increase biomass concentra-
tion and productivity, but exclusive heterotrophy is considered to
be more costly than photoautotrophy. The commercial viability
of algal-based biofuels ultimately depends on the economics with
the key factors being substrate cost, lipid yield and the product
quality obtained from the downstream processing (Yang et al.,
2006). The cost of the organic carbon substrate has been estimated
to be up to 50% of the total medium cost used in algal cultivation
(Cheng et al., 2009). The ﬁnal price of biodiesel has also been re-
ported to be dependent on the feedstock cost which accounts for
60–75% of the total cost of biodiesel fuel (Canakci and Sanli, 2008).
With biofuels being a low value product, the cost of feedstock
production must be reduced to the minimum to make it econom-
ically feasible and competitive on a large-scale. Mixotrophic
cultivation of microalgae, where photosynthetic growth is supple-
mented with inexpensive carbon-rich substrates such as carbohy-
drates from industrial and agricultural wastes and crude glycerol
from biodiesel production, could potentially reduce the cost of
algal biomass production (Liang et al., 2009; Abreu et al., 2012).
Mixotrophic cultivation has also been shown to improve the
growth rate and lipid production in microalgae resulting in a short-
er growth cycle and increased biomass and storage molecule
productivity (Lee, 2001; Liang et al., 2009; Wan et al., 2011). Exper-
imental studies have shown that the maximum growth rate and
cell concentration of some microalgae (e.g. Spirulina platensis, Chlo-
rella vulgaris and Haematococcus pluvialis) growing under mixo-
trophic conditions corresponds to the sum of the autotrophic and

respectively (Lee, 2001). The biochemical composition of algal bio-
mass is hugely dependent on the cultivation conditions; mixo-
trophic microalgae have been shown to have higher productivity
of lipid, starch and proteins than microalgae grown under photo-
autotrophic conditions (Xu et al., 2004; Garc´ia et al., 2005; Abreu
et al., 2012). Furthermore, when compared to photoautotrophic
growth conditions, mixotrophic cultivation is associated with low-
er energy cost due to its relatively lower requirements for light
intensity (Abreu et al., 2012).
Microalgal growth and their biochemical composition are
strongly affected by environmental conditions such as nutrient
availability and light. Therefore, mathematical models that have
the ability to predict the dynamics of algal cultures under different
growth conditions will aid optimisation of process performance,
operating conditions and scaling-up cultivation systems for com-
mercial algal-based technology. Kinetic modelling based on the
well established Droop, Monod and Logistic models has tradition-
ally been used to predict algal growth in response to the substrate
concentration such as nitrogen (Smit, 2002), phosphorus (Yao
et al., 2011). Some researchers have also focused mainly on the
effect of light intensity on photosynthesis, growth and storage
molecule accumulation in microalgae (Fernandez et al., 1997;
Yun and Park, 2003), whilst others have developed models to
predict both biomass growth and lipid accumulation under a single
growth condition e.g. photoautotrophy or heterotrophy (Yang
et al., 2011; Packer et al., 2011; Quinn et al., 2011; Tevatia et al.,
2012). However, there is currently no mathematical model avail-
able to describe algal growth dynamics and storage molecule
synthesis

conditions.
In this work, a mathematical model is established for growth of
the green alga C. vulgaris, including storage molecule production
and nutrient consumption under mixotrophic growth conditions
with three limiting factors (nitrogen, carbon, light) based on exist-
ing model frameworks in the literature. The ability of the proposed
mixotrophic model to predict the dynamics of algal cultures over a
wide range of growth conditions was also explored. Photoautotro-
phic growth of C. vulgaris was achieved through some modiﬁca-
tions of the base case model by setting the concentration of the
organic carbon source to zero (qc = 0). Sensitivity analysis was con-
ducted to determine how and to what extent the changes in key
parameters affected the model performance (see Supplementary
material for more details).
2. Modelling method
2.1. Algal cell composition and carbon balance
In this work, algal biomass (dry cell weight) is divided into two
components (i.e. a two compartment model) as presented in
Fig. 1a: the functional biomass (X) (i.e. non TAG or starch) and
the storage molecule (S) in the form of TAG lipid and starch. Hence,
the total algal biomass concentration is the sum of the two compo-
nents, X + S. Fig. 1b shows a schematic overview of the carbon ﬂow
balance in an algal cell. The main energy and carbon sources are
from photosynthesis (pX) and the organic substrate (qcX). The
functional biomass growth (X) is regulated by the availability of
intracellular nitrogen concentration (c), which here is described
by the Droop equation. When all the nitrogen nutrients has been
consumed and the minimum nitrogen cell quota, qn (deﬁned as
the internal nitrogen concentration where cells cease to grow) is
reached, excess ﬁxed carbon is channelled to the production of
storage molecules (starch granules and TAG bodies). Not all the
ﬁxed carbon is incorporated into the total algal biomass (X + S) be-
cause some is lost as a result of various metabolic activities and cell
maintenance, essentially via respiration. In this paper, carbon
losses via respiration (RM) are taken into consideration.
2.2. Model development
The model was constructed based on the following general
assumptions: (a) culture conditions (pH, micronutrients, CO2 mass
transfer, etc.) are optimised, (b) temperature is constant, (c) uni-
form mixing is attained such that mixing dynamics does not dras-
tically affect the microalgal growth rate, (d) phosphorus is not a
limiting nutrient, (e) dry weight of the storage molecule (TAG
and starch) is proportional to its dry weight of carbon. Based on
these assumptions, a model is proposed to describe mixotrophic
growth in a batch algal culture, although with suitable modiﬁca-
tions to the base equations, the model could also be applied to
other growth systems. A combination of ﬁve ordinary differential
equations (ODEs) comprising ﬁve state variables is used to describe
the functional algal biomass concentration, X (g dw m3), storage

2.2.1. Functional algal biomass (X)
The growth of functional biomass is limited either by nitrogen
(N) or light. N limitation is accounted for using the well established
cell quota (Droop) model which assumes biomass growth is depen-
dent on intracellular nutrient quota rather than the external con-
centration of nutrient in the culture medium. Therefore, the rate
of carbon ﬁxed into functional biomass X is moderated by a factor
of (1  qn/Qn). The nitrogen cell quota Qn is deﬁned as the mass of
internal nitrogen per total mass of biomass, while the minimum
nitrogen cell quota qn is the internal nitrogen concentration where
cells cease to grow. The growth rate not limited by nitrogen (i.e.
when Qn >> qn) is the sum of the autotrophic (light) and the hetero-
trophic (carbon) growth rates. In order to incorporate light, it is as-

2.2.2. Storage molecule (S)
Algal cells experience rapid growth in nutrient sufﬁcient med-
ium until growth-limiting nutrients (typically N) become depleted.
Once growth becomes limited, excess ﬁxed carbon can accumulate
in storage products in the form of starch and/or TAG lipid, which
are very important for survival under unfavourable conditions
(e.g. low nutrients, high light) (Schenk et al., 2008; Scott et al.,
2010; Siaut et al., 2011). As Qn ? qn, there is a decrease in the
functional biomass growth rate and carbon ﬁxation becomes
uncoupled from growth, but may proceed at rates exceeding the
C requirement for metabolic activities in N-sufﬁcient algal cells
(Packer et al., 2011). It is assumed that excess carbon and energy
is channelled to synthesise and accumulate both TAGs and starch
molecules such that increase in total biomass is due to de novo syn-
thesis of storage products. Taking the algal cell as a control volume,
a balance on the inﬂux of carbon gives the storage molecule pro-
duction within the cell as all of the carbon ﬁxed via photosynthesis
and organic C uptake minus that allocated for functional biomass
growth (Eq. (2)). Since the storage molecule acts as a carbon sink
under nitrogen limited conditions, in this study, the dry weight
of the storage molecule is assumed to be proportional to its dry
weight of carbon.

2.2.3. Chlorophyll content (B)
In this model, chlorophyll synthesis is considered because it
plays an important role in photosynthetic reactions and is also af-
fected by the availability of nitrogen. Nitrogen is a structural ele-

the formation of chloroplasts and accumulation of chlorophyll in
phytoplankton (Tucker, 2004). According to the work carried out
by Geider et al. (1998), the chlorophyll content of many microalgae
is linked directly to N uptake (qn) from the culture medium. This
suggests that the kinetic conversion of inorganic nitrogen to organ-
ic nitrogen within the algal cell is relatively fast. It is assumed that

ised per unit N assimilated. The proportion of N uptake (qn) dedi-
cated to chlorophyll synthesis is taken to be the fraction h of the

2.2.4. Extracellular nitrogen (N)
In this model, it is assumed that the main limiting nutrient to
algal growth is nitrogen. Following the approach of Geider et al.
(1998), the external nitrogen concentration is modelled based on
N uptake (qn) and assimilation whilst neglecting the effect of tem-
perature. The N uptake rate incorporates the metabolic costs of
reducing nitrate present in the medium to ammonium as well as
incorporating ammonium into the biomass (Geider et al., 1998).
The Michaelis–Menten kinetic equation is used to express the
uptake rate of nitrogen as a function of extracellular N concentra-
tion, characterised by a negative feedback which is linearly depen-
dent on Qn (Geider et al., 1998). The nitrogen consumption rate, qn,
decreases linearly with intracellular concentration of nitrogen Qn,
such that qn becomes vnm for Qn = qn and zero for Qn = qnm (Geider
et al., 1998). A saturation parameter (qnm) accounts for the maxi-
mum N quota that can be stored within an algal cell. The maximum
and minimum cell quota (qnm and qn) provide a wide range for
nitrogen storage within the algal cells.

2.2.7. Carbon quota (Qc)
There is loss of ﬁxed carbon atom within algal cells due to var-
ious metabolic activities such as the generation of usable energy
(e.g. ATP, NADPH and NADH) and metabolic intermediates (e.g.
enzymatic proteins and ribonucleic acids). The carbon present
within an algal cell (XQc) is therefore dependent on the C uptake
from the growth medium and ﬁxed by photosynthesis, less that
lost, modelled here with a respiration term. The respiration losses
crudely account for the metabolic costs of growth and biosynthesis
and the cost of repair and cell maintenance, which are reported in
plants as well as algae (Lambers et al., 2005). It is assumed that
only the starch compounds are used for respiration. The mainte-
nance respiration rate (RM) can be expressed as a percentage of
photosynthetic rate (Quinn et al., 2011); here, 10% is assumed.

3.1. Deﬁnitions

were investigated, under different nitrogen concentrations. Nitro-
gen-sufﬁcient conditions are deﬁned as algal cultivation in 3N-

of the nitrogen level employed for nitrogen-sufﬁcient growth. For
mixotrophic growth, the culture medium contains 0.5 g/l glucose
used as an organic carbon source. This low concentration of
glucose was considered in order to reduce the embodied energy
associated with glucose production and subsequently reduce the
overall environmental impact of algal biofuel production.

from Culture Collection of Algae and Protozoa (CCAP, Oban,
Scotland) were grown in 6  1000 ml conical ﬂask. Cells were
cultivated autotrophically in 3N-BBM+V medium made up of inor-
ganic salts (CCAP). The ﬂasks were placed in an incubator (Infors

Flasks were aerated with CO2-enriched air (5% v/v CO2) via a
0.2 lm sterile ﬁlter. Cultures were continuously illuminated using
white ﬂuorescent lamps under a light intensity of 80 lmol/m2-s
measured at the base of the ﬂasks using a Skye light meter with

grown under nitrogen-sufﬁcient autotrophic growth conditions

experiments were independently set up in triplicates; C. vulgaris
grown in 3N-BBM+V or 0.5N-BBM+V for autotrophic growth and
C. vulgaris grown in 3N-BBM+V or 0.5N-BBM+V both containing
0.5 g/l glucose for mixotrophic growth.
3.3. Stock culture transfer to media containing different nitrogen
concentration with or without glucose
Once the culture had reached the exponential growth phase
corresponding to an optical density (OD750) of 1.2 (equivalent
to 0.4 g/l dry cell weight), the cultures from the six ﬂasks were har-
vested and merged on the same day (day 0) for each experimental
set up. 50 ml aliquots of the merged culture were placed into ster-
ile 50 ml screw-cap plastic tubes and centrifuged at a speed of
600g for 10 min at 25 C using a Beckman Coulter, Avanti J-26 XP
centrifuge. The supernatant was discarded and 20 ml sterile deion-
ised water was added to the pellet of algal cells in each centrifuge
tube, gently shaken to wash and remove all traces of the original
medium. The suspension was centrifuged as above and the pellets
were then re-suspended in 50 ml of new media containing various
known concentrations of nitrate with or without glucose depend-

0.2 g/l for each of the growth experiment, the pellets were diluted
by 2-fold. Cultures with similar medium composition for each set
of experiment were merged into a sterile beaker from which
50 ml of algal culture with a depth of 30 mm was transferred into
100 ml glass ﬂasks for batch cultivation. The ﬂasks were placed in a
closed incubator as above enriched with a 5% CO2 atmosphere
within the growth cabinet. Three 100 ml ﬂasks containing cultures
for each set of experiment were harvested every other day for
20 days after day 0 (day of inoculation) and used for a single time
point analysis.
3.4. Analytical measurement
Optical density (OD) was measured using a Thermo Spectronic
UV1 spectrophotometer at a wavelength of 750 nm and Fisher-
brand disposable polystyrene cuvettes. For dry cell weight mea-
surement, 20 ml of aliquots were harvested and centrifuged at
5000g for 5 min at 25 C. The supernatant was discarded and the
pellets were washed in 20 ml of deionised water, re-centrifuged
and re-suspended in 5 ml deionised water. The suspension was
then ﬁltered through a pre-weighed 45 lm glass–ﬁbre ﬁlter paper
(Whatman GF/C, USA). The ﬁlter paper was dried in a Gallenkamp
hotbox oven at 80 C for 48 h before re-weighing to determine the
dry cell weight. Total chlorophyll (a + b) was extracted by centri-
fuging 200–500 lL algal culture, discarding the supernatant and
re-suspending the pellets in 1 ml dimethylformamide (DMF). The
samples were vortexed for 15 min and the absorbance of the ex-
tract was determined at 665 nm and 647 nm using a Thermo Spec-
tronic UV1 spectrophotometer. Total chlorophyll was calculated
using the equation by Inskeep and Bloom (1985).
Nitrate analysis was performed with a commercial Fluka
Analytical 37408 Aquanal-plus Nitrate (NO3) kit supplied by Sig-
ma–Aldrich. With a pre-determined calibration curve, nitrate
concentration was determined at an absorbance of 515 nm accord-
ing to the manufacturer’s manual instructions. Total starch concen-

4. Results and discussion
4.1. Algal growth and storage molecule production under different
culture mode
Algal growth under different culture conditions with varying ini-
tial nitrogen concentrations is shown in Fig. 2a. There is clear differ-
ence between mixotrophic and autotrophic growth conditions
under different nitrogen concentrations despite starting with the
same size of inocula. Under mixotrophic conditions, the overall
growth of algal biomass was signiﬁcantly greater compared to
autotrophic growth conditions for the same starting nitrogen con-
centration. This is presumably because the added glucose allows
the accumulation of algal biomass with less energy input than
purely inorganic CO2 ﬁxation. Similar results showing higher
biomass productivity for other strains of C. vulgaris cultivated under
mixotrophic growth conditions have also been reported (Liang et al.,
2009; Abreu et al., 2012). With the presence of glucose, biomass
yield was about 1.5 times greater than that from autotrophic growth
under nitrogen sufﬁcient conditions during exponential growth
phase. Overall, the growth of C. vulgaris under nitrogen limited con-
ditions was signiﬁcantly lower when compared with nitrogen sufﬁ-
cient conditions for both mixotrophic and autotrophic culture
mode. The maximum biomass density (3.5 g/l) and the highest
biomass productivity (222 ± 10 mg l1 day1) were obtained when
the algae cells were grown mixotrophically using 0.5 g/l glucose
under nitrogen sufﬁcient conditions as presented in Table 2. The
biomass cell density and productivity for C. vulgaris cultivated under
different growth conditions investigated in this study are summa-

molecule (sum of starch and TAG) production as measured during
the duration of the experiment. The maximum storage molecule
density (1.44 g/l) was observed under mixotrophic nitrogen stress

4.3. Model parameter estimation
Initial estimates for the model parameters were obtained from
the literature. These parameter values were then numerically opti-
mised in order to obtain a best ﬁt of the model to experimental
data using the fminsearch routine in Matlab program with the
objective functions as the residual sum of squares for total dry cell
weight, storage molecule content, chlorophyll content and extra-
cellular nitrogen concentration. This MATLAB optimisation func-
tion utilises the simplex search algorithm described in Lagarias
et al. (1998). The parameter values and ranges determined by this
algorithm are realistic and consistent with the literature (see
Supplementary material). Parameters such as the culture depth,
incident light intensity, initial biomass density and nutrient
concentration for the experiments were constants in the model
for all the growth conditions considered in this work. A summary
of the model input and parameter values used in this study is pre-
sented in Table 3.
4.4. Validation of the growth and storage molecule model
Fig. 4 shows the model results plotted against the experimental
data for C. vulgaris. As observed in Fig. 4a and d, the model qualita-
tively and quantitatively reﬂects the biomass growth trends for the
time scale employed over the entire duration of the experiments.
The maximum standard deviation from the predicted biomass
versus the actual measured biomass over the duration of the
experiments was calculated to be 0.078 g/l, indicating that the
model accurately simulates the biomass growth in this system.
The model is observed to be able to predict bulk biomass growth
under both nitrogen sufﬁcient and limited conditions with a max-
imum overestimation of 0.086 g/l and underestimation of 0.04 g/l
and maximum over prediction of 3.2% for the four set of growth
experiments.
The experimental data and model predictions for storage
molecule density and percentage of biomass are presented in
Fig. 4b, c, e and f. The model predicts the storage molecule percent-
age level of the biomass to reach a maximum of 75% after 20 days
under nitrogen limited conditions for both mixotrophic and auto-
trophic growth, a value which is consistent with the experimental
data (Fig. 6b and d). It is observed that the model captures the
trend of storage molecule production in algal cells for all the
growth conditions under investigation. Experimental results show
that on average, there are about 3 times as much starch as TAG
molecules until day 8, where after starch remained constant or be-
gan to reduce whilst TAG levels increased markedly. A different
model separating lipid and starch accumulation in algal cells under
mixotrophic conditions would be required to accurately represent
each biochemical composition of the microalgae.
4.5. Substrate consumption
Fig. 5 shows the time course of substrate consumption from the
microalgal culture medium for nitrogen and organic carbon. Under
nitrogen deﬁcient conditions, it is observed that nitrogen is con-
sumed quickly by the algae and becomes limiting after day 4 for
both mixotrophic and autotrophic growth conditions (Fig. 5a and
b). Although the extracellular nitrogen is depleted quickly in the
medium, the cells continued to grow over the duration of the
experiments as shown in Fig. 2a. This luxury uptake of nutrients
and storage for later growth is a well established phenomenon in
phytoplankton (Droop, 1983) hence, the assumption implicit in
the model that algal growth depends not on the extracellular nitro-
gen concentration in the culture medium but on the intracellular
nitrogen content. Nitrogen uptake proceeded gradually under suf-
ﬁcient conditions but was completely consumed after day 20 for
both mixotrophic and autotrophic cultures. For mixotrophic
growth, glucose consumption was faster during algae cultivation
under nitrogen sufﬁcient conditions and was completely ex-
hausted after 12 days of inoculation. This observation could be
attributed to the high biomass concentration resulting from the
sufﬁcient extracellular nitrogen in the culture which enhanced
continuous algae growth and subsequent glucose uptake from
the medium. In contrast, under nitrogen limited conditions of incu-
bation, the algae did not consume or remove a signiﬁcant amount
of glucose from the culture medium (Fig. 5c). The model ﬁtted the
experimental data for both nitrogen and glucose consumption in C.
vulgaris cultures under the different growth conditions as pre-
sented in Fig. 5.
4.6. Chlorophyll formation
The inﬂuence of different nutritional modes on chlorophyll for-
mation is presented in Fig. 6. It is observed that the percentage
chlorophyll per dry cell weight declines sharply in the nitrogen
deﬁcient culture medium after day 2 when the nitrogen is com-
pletely exhausted, reaching less than 2% of the total dry cell weight
in day 20 for both autotrophic and mixotrophic growth conditions.
Chlorophyll synthesis is linked to nitrogen uptake and has been
linearly correlated to cellular proteins (Bernard, 2011). Therefore,
low extracellular nitrogen availability leads to less cellular protein
synthesis, which is associated with a decrease in rubisco produc-
tion, giving a negative feedback for chlorophyll production in mic-
roalgae (Packer et al., 2011). The feedback built into the model is
able to accurately reﬂect the phenomena of chlorophyll formation
under different nitrogen concentrations. Under nitrogen sufﬁcient
medium, chlorophyll formation increases over the ﬁrst two days
and then gradually decreases to 3.7% and 2.8% of the total dry cell
weight in day 20 for autotrophic and mixotrophic culture mode
respectively. The observed experimental pattern for chlorophyll
formation in the algal cells is accurately captured by the model
simulation results for all four sets of cultivation mode under inves-
tigation as shown in Fig. 6. The maximum chlorophyll content

4.7. Model limitations and implications
One apparent limitation of the model is the fact that a single set
of parameters could not be used to describe the culture behaviour
under both high and low nitrogen concentration. The best ﬁt of the
model to each set of growth data resulted in different values for the
most sensitive parameters, while the non-sensitive parameters
were relatively similar. Nonetheless, the parameter values and
ranges are realistic and agree well with published data. It is impor-
tant to state that a global optimisation routine in MATLAB was
used to obtain a single set of parameters which describes the
dynamics of algal culture under all the four growth conditions
investigated. However, this attempt could not generate a single
set of parameters under the different nitrogen cultures. A reason-
able explanation for this result could be due to the two extreme
N concentrations used in this study. The 3N culture medium had

5. Conclusion
A kinetic model was developed to describe the dynamics of C.
vulgaris cultures as a function of nitrogen and light under both
mixotrophic and autotrophic conditions. Experimentally, it was
found that under nitrogen limitation, starch accumulation initially
occurred at a faster rate, followed by TAG accumulation once
starch levels reached a maximum. The proposed model captures
the experimental data well for all the growth conditions investi-
gated. This study provides a scientiﬁc platform for understanding
algal metabolism that would be relevant for bioreactor design, pro-
cess control and optimisation, and scale-up of cultivation systems
for commercial-scale production of algal-based products.
